title: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species sometimes have habits that do not match their structure, such as upland geese with webbed feet that rarely enter water or ground-living woodpeckers, showing that habits can change before structure changes.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In such cases, and many others could be given, habits have changed without a corresponding change of structure.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Species with habits widely different from those of their allies.”. Scope: birds and other animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-06: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Current behaviour and retained anatomy can be documented directly in many species. Existing data support the existence claim, but historical precedence usually requires uncertain ancestral reconstruction.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify species whose observed habitat use or behaviour differs from that predicted by homologous structures and close relatives, then reconstruct whether behavioural shifts precede structural evolution. Repeated behavioural mismatch with retained ancestral anatomy supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Structure-function mismatch requires an explicit expectation model.

Present-day mismatch does not by itself establish the temporal order of habit and structural change.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Diet, foraging stratum, and locomotor morphology are already tabulated for birds and mammals, so a mismatch census is a feasible comparative analysis. That census can establish that discordant combinations occur, which is the existential pattern. It cannot order the changes in time, because structure lagging habit and habit lagging structure look the same in a static table.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score species whose diet or foraging habitat conflicts with locomotor morphology, such as webbed feet with terrestrial foraging or climbing morphology with ground foraging. Repeated mismatches would confirm that habit and structure can come apart; a scoring rule under which essentially no species mismatch would refute the existential claim. A static mismatch does not show that habit changed first.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
EltonTraits records species-level habits, not individual flexibility.

The order of change, habit before structure, is not identified by a present-day mismatch.

What counts as a mismatch between habit and structure needs an explicit coding rule.
